subject: chem
title: Group 2
subtitle: Reactions, trends and uses of Group 2 elements and compounds.
concept: Group 2 elements (Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba) lose 2 electrons to form M²⁺ ions; reactivity increases down the group as IE decreases.
Group 2 oxides and hydroxides are bases; they neutralise acids and are used industrially.
Solubility trends: sulfates become less soluble down the group; hydroxides become more soluble.

notes.heading: Reactions of Group 2 Metals
items: Reaction with oxygen: 2M + O₂ → 2MO (burns brightly; Mg burns intensely white).
Reaction with water: Mg reacts slowly with hot water/steam (MgO + H₂); Ca, Sr, Ba react with cold water → M(OH)₂ + H₂.
Reaction with dilute acid: M + H₂SO₄ → MSO₄ + H₂ (MgSO₄ soluble; CaSO₄ sparingly soluble — may slow reaction due to insoluble layer).
Ca reacts more vigorously than Mg — lower IE, metal is more easily oxidised.

notes.heading: Oxides and Hydroxides
items: All Group 2 oxides are basic: MO + H₂O → M(OH)₂ (CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂, exothermic — quicklime/slaked lime).
MgO: refractory material (very high MP ~2852°C); used in furnace linings.
Ca(OH)₂: used to neutralise acidic soil, treat sewage, make glass.
CaCO₃ (limestone): quarried; heated to give CaO (lime) — used in steelmaking and pH control of soil.
Thermal decomposition: MCO₃ → MO + CO₂. Ease of decomposition decreases down the group (higher T needed for BaCO₃).

notes.heading: Solubility Trends
items: Group 2 sulfates: MgSO₄ (soluble) → CaSO₄ (sparingly) → SrSO₄ (insoluble) → BaSO₄ (insoluble). Solubility decreases down the group.
Group 2 hydroxides: Mg(OH)₂ (sparingly soluble) → Ca(OH)₂ (slightly) → Ba(OH)₂ (soluble). Solubility increases down the group.
BaSO₄: used in barium meal (X-ray contrast agent) — insoluble so not absorbed; opaque to X-rays.
Test for SO₄²⁻ ions: add BaCl₂(aq) acidified with HCl → white precipitate of BaSO₄ (HCl prevents carbonate/sulfite interference).

definitions.body: A reaction in which a compound breaks down when heated into simpler substances.
Sulfates become less soluble down Group 2; hydroxides become more soluble down Group 2.

workedExamples.q: Explain the trend in reactivity of Group 2 metals with water down the group.

steps.text: Ca reacts vigorously with cold water; Mg only reacts with hot water/steam. Reactivity increases Ca > Mg.
Down the group, atomic radius increases and shielding increases → outer electrons further from nucleus → lower first and second IE.
Easier to lose the 2 outer electrons → more reactive metal → reacts more readily with water.

mistakes: Saying Group 2 hydroxide solubility decreases down the group — it increases (Ba(OH)₂ is most soluble).
Using dilute HNO₃ instead of HCl when testing for sulfate — HNO₃ is an oxidising acid that can interfere.
tips: Barium meal uses BaSO₄ — INSOLUBLE, not absorbed → safe to ingest; BaCl₂ would be toxic.
Thermal stability of carbonates: increases down group (more difficult to decompose BaCO₃ than MgCO₃).
Flame colours: Mg (no characteristic); Ca (brick red); Sr (crimson); Ba (pale green).

flashcards.q: What is the trend in solubility of Group 2 hydroxides down the group?
flashcards.a: Solubility increases — Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble; Ba(OH)₂ is soluble.

flashcards.q: Why is BaSO₄ used in barium meals (X-ray imaging)?
flashcards.a: BaSO₄ is insoluble and not absorbed through the gut (non-toxic); it is opaque to X-rays, showing up the digestive tract.

flashcards.q: Write the equation for thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate.
Why does reactivity of Group 2 metals increase down the group?
flashcards.a: Atomic radius increases; outer electrons are more shielded and further from nucleus → lower IE → easier to lose 2e⁻.

flashcards.q: What is the test for sulfate ions?
flashcards.a: Add BaCl₂(aq) acidified with HCl → white precipitate of BaSO₄ (insoluble).

flashcards.q: What is the trend in Group 2 sulfate solubility?
flashcards.a: Decreases down the group: MgSO₄ soluble; BaSO₄ insoluble.

questions.q: Which Group 2 hydroxide is most soluble?
questions.exp: Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group — Ba(OH)₂ is the most soluble.

questions.q: What is formed when CaO reacts with water?
questions.exp: CaO (quicklime) + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (slaked lime); exothermic reaction.

questions.q: The trend in thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates down the group is:
questions.exp: Thermal stability increases down the group — BaCO₃ requires higher temperatures to decompose than MgCO₃.

questions.q: How is sulfate ion confirmed in solution?
opts: Add BaCl₂(aq) acidified with HCl → white precipitate
questions.exp: BaCl₂ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄ (white precipitate); acidified with HCl to remove interfering CO₃²⁻ and SO₃²⁻.

questions.q: Why does barium sulfate (not barium chloride) used in X-ray imaging?
opts: BaSO₄ is more opaque to X-rays
BaSO₄ is insoluble and non-toxic; BaCl₂ is soluble and toxic
BaSO₄ dissolves slowly in the stomach
questions.exp: BaSO₄ is insoluble — not absorbed into the bloodstream, so it's non-toxic. BaCl₂ is soluble and would be toxic.

questions.q: Which Group 2 sulfate is used in barium meals for X-ray imaging?
questions.exp: BaSO₄ is completely insoluble in water (and in body fluids), so it is non-toxic. It is opaque to X-rays, outlining the gastrointestinal tract. More soluble barium salts are toxic.

questions.q: Down Group 2, the solubility of hydroxides:
questions.exp: Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group: Mg(OH)₂ is almost insoluble; Ca(OH)₂ is slightly soluble; Ba(OH)₂ is the most soluble. This is because lattice enthalpy decreases more than hydration enthalpy.

questions.q: What is produced when magnesium burns in oxygen?
questions.exp: Burning Mg in air produces MgO (from O₂) and Mg₃N₂ (from N₂ in air). In pure oxygen, only MgO forms. The reaction is highly exothermic with an intense white flame.

questions.q: Calcium hydroxide solution (limewater) turns milky when CO₂ is bubbled through. What forms?
questions.exp: Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l). The white precipitate of insoluble CaCO₃ makes the solution milky. This is the limewater test for CO₂.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates?
opts: MgCO₃ is the most thermally stable
BaCO₃ requires the highest temperature to decompose
All Group 2 carbonates decompose at the same temperature
CaCO₃ is more stable than BaCO₃
questions.exp: Thermal stability increases down Group 2. Larger cations are less polarising, so they distort the carbonate ion less and more energy is needed to decompose it. BaCO₃ decomposes at ~1360 °C vs MgCO₃ at ~350 °C.

questions.q: What happens when calcium reacts with cold water?
opts: Vigorous reaction producing H₂ and Ca(OH)₂
Slow reaction producing CaO and H₂
questions.exp: Ca(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g). Calcium reacts steadily (not explosively) with cold water, unlike Group 1 metals. The reaction is faster than Mg with cold water but slower than Ba.

questions.q: Down Group 2, the first ionisation energy:
opts: Decreases because atomic radius increases and shielding increases
questions.exp: Atomic radius increases down Group 2 (more electron shells) and shielding increases, so the outer electron is less strongly attracted to the nucleus. First ionisation energy decreases from Mg to Ba.

questions.q: Magnesium oxide is used as an antacid and refractory lining. This is due to its:
opts: High solubility and low melting point
Basic nature and very high melting point
Acidic nature and high melting point
Neutral character and low melting point
questions.exp: MgO is a basic oxide (reacts with acids), making it useful as an antacid. Its ionic lattice is very strongly held together (small, highly charged ions → high lattice energy) giving a very high melting point (~2852 °C) — ideal for refractory linings.

questions.q: The solubility of Group 2 sulfates down the group:
questions.exp: Solubility of Group 2 sulfates decreases down the group: MgSO₄ is soluble; CaSO₄ is sparingly soluble; SrSO₄ and BaSO₄ are insoluble. The trend is opposite to that of the hydroxides.

questions.q: Which Group 2 element reacts most vigorously with water?
questions.exp: Reactivity increases down Group 2 as ionisation energy decreases. Barium reacts most vigorously with cold water. Magnesium only reacts appreciably with steam, and very slowly with cold water.

questions.q: Which Group 2 hydroxide is least soluble?
questions.exp: Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases DOWN the group. Mg(OH)₂ (least soluble) → Ba(OH)₂ (most soluble).

questions.q: What is observed when magnesium reacts with cold water?
questions.exp: Mg reacts very slowly with cold water (unlike Ca which reacts readily). It reacts quickly with steam to give MgO + H₂.

questions.q: Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating. What are the products?
questions.exp: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (thermal decomposition). Thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases down the group.

questions.q: Which Group 2 sulfate is insoluble in water?
questions.exp: BaSO₄ is virtually insoluble (Ksp ≈ 10⁻¹⁰). It is used in barium meals as it is safe to ingest and opaque to X-rays. Solubility decreases down the group.

questions.q: Barium chloride solution is added to a sulfate solution. What forms?
questions.exp: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s) — white precipitate. This is the test for sulfate ions.

questions.q: Why does reactivity of Group 2 metals increase down the group?
opts: Increasing atomic radius and decreasing ionisation energy
questions.exp: Larger atoms have more shielded outer electrons; ionisation energy falls, so metals lose electrons more easily — higher reactivity.

questions.q: Which Group 2 compound is used to neutralise excess stomach acid?
questions.exp: MgO (or Mg(OH)₂ suspension) is used as an antacid — it neutralises HCl in stomach acid: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O.

questions.q: Limewater (Ca(OH)₂ solution) turns milky when CO₂ is bubbled through. The precipitate is:
questions.exp: Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O. CaCO₃ is insoluble — turns the solution milky. Excess CO₂ re-dissolves it as Ca(HCO₃)₂.

questions.q: The thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases down the group because:
opts: Larger cations polarise the carbonate ion less
questions.exp: Larger cations (lower charge density) polarise and distort the carbonate ion less → more energy needed to decompose → higher thermal stability.

questions.q: What is the product when calcium reacts with water?
questions.exp: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. Calcium reacts readily with cold water, forming calcium hydroxide (sparingly soluble) and hydrogen gas.

recall: State the trend in reactivity of Group 2 metals and explain it.
Describe the reactions of Group 2 metals with oxygen and water.
Compare the solubility trends of Group 2 sulfates and hydroxides.
Explain the use of BaSO₄ in barium meals.
Describe the industrial uses of CaO and Ca(OH)₂.
